1.text: MARRIAGE AMONG THE REINDEER CHUKCHEE. — With the Reindeer Chuk-

2.text: chee no man can live a tolerable life without having a separate house of his

3.text: own and a woman to take care of it. The sleeping-room of the Chukchee

4.text: “genuine house” is exceedingly small, and there is no extra place in it even

5.text: for a brother or a near relative. Thus a man living in another man’s camp,

6.text: and dependent on the herd of the master, must still have a house of his own;

7.text: otherwise, when he comes home for a rest, he may be obliged to sleep in

8.text: the open just in the worst part of the season, when nobody would be willing

9.text: to change places with him. He will also have no one to mend his clothes

10.text: and to see that they are dried, because the women of the master’s tent will

11.text: have plenty to do for their own people. If he is not married, and has a

12.text: mother, she will be able to take care of his home; but even a mother’s care

13.text: is not sufficient. In the depth of winter, when going away with the herd from

14.text: the winter quarters, he should take with him a young woman, strong of body,

15.text: and light of foot, to take care of his travelling-tent, and also, in the case of

16.text: need, to lend a hand with the restive animals. A sister, of course, may do

17.text: that, but sisters are apt to go away to other men’s houses. Sometimes one

18.text: of the master’s daughters may go with a young unmarried herdsman of her

19.text: father, but a trip like this will lead to marriage. Among the motives for

20.text: marriage must also be mentioned the idea of the necessity of continuing the

21.text: family line, and of not allowing it to be broken off. This idea is well-expressed

22.text: in one tale, where a sister says to her only brother, “Go seek a wife for

23.text: yourself; take her and generate children, lest our family life be extinguished

24.text: in later years.¹ Words like these are found in many tales.

25.text: Therefore each Reindeer Chukchee, when he feels himself to be “with

26.text: full-grown body” (uwiˊk-ɪpčɪˊtkuk), endeavors to be married and have a home

27.text: of his own. A man full-grown and unmarried is despised by the people, and

28.text: in reality is looked upon as a good-for-nothing (tŭmñeˊ-leiˊvulɪn), a lounger, a

29.text: tramp, idly wandering from camp to camp.² I shall speak of such men further

30.text: on; but even among them, many have a wife, and wander about with her,

31.text: or leave her for a time in another person’s house. Besides this, there are

32.text: men who cannot have a wife because of some grave physical defect which

33.text: hinders sexual life. Thus, the Chukchee told me that sometimes, when a

34.text: mother was neglectful of her infant, and did not change frequently enough

36.text: ² According to E. Westermarck, on the authority of Armstrong (Discovery of the North-West Passage,

37.text: p. 192), among the Eskimo a person who does not marry is looked upon almost as an unnatural being, or at

38.text: any rate is disdained (E. Westermarck, History of Human Marriage, p. 136).
